card.name: Cendrawasih
card.tagline: A vivid Balinese duet depicting the theatrical courtship of birds of paradise.
card.profile: Cendrawasih is a contemporary Balinese dance performed by two female dancers portraying male and female birds of paradise in a dramatic courtship ritual. Originally conceived in a different form by I Gde Manik in Buleleng during the 1920s, the present choreography was created by N. L. N. Swasthi Wijaya Bandem in 1988. Dancers wear Pandji-style feathered headdresses and long skirts with pink stripes, which they spread and flutter to emulate glowing wings. Unique among Balinese dance traditions, Cendrawasih incorporates standing en pointe and dynamic skirt-work to mimic avian flight.
card.insight: First choreographed in 1988 by N. L. N. Swasthi Wijaya Bandem, a single performance of the Cendrawasih duet burns 40 calories as dancers flutter their feathered skirts en pointe.

card.profile_long:
### Origins and History
An early dance named Cendrawasih was created by I Gde Manik in the 1920s within the Sawan subdistrict of Buleleng Regency, Bali—the same historic heartland that birthed classic pieces such as Trunajaya, Wirangjaya, and Palawakya. However, that early 1920s iteration differed significantly from the modern repertory. The current rendition of Cendrawasih stems from choreography designed by N. L. N. Swasthi Wijaya Bandem, premiered in 1988. Inspired by the bird of paradise, known in Indonesian as burung cendrawasih and in Balinese as manuk dewata ("the bird of the gods"), the piece distills the avian rituals of courtship into formal theatrical movement. Cendrawasih forms part of a broader lineage of bird-inspired Balinese dances alongside Manuk Rawa and Belibis.

### How It Is Danced
The dance is staged as an intimate duet between two women: one portraying the male bird of paradise and the other portraying the female. Together, they perform a stylized mating ritual characterized by playful fluttering, flirting, and bird-like motions. Choreographers and individual performers are permitted to introduce their own interpretations within the canonical frame. Unlike most classical Balinese dance forms, Cendrawasih introduces distinct physical techniques such as standing en pointe and using trailing costume elements to simulate outstretched wings. Fast running passes make the flowing skirts ripple, conveying the vivid visual impression of birds taking flight.

### Music and Instruments
While specific gamelan orchestra arrangements for Cendrawasih are not detailed in the sources, Balinese bird dances traditionally rely on dynamic gamelan accompaniment. The music matches the courtship story, shifting between delicate melodic sections during intimate flirting gestures and rapid, driving percussive rhythms that propel the dancers through swift flights across the stage.

### Costume and Setting
The visually striking costumes are central to the performance narrative. Dancers wear feathered Pandji-style headdresses alongside long flowing skirts or scarves adorned with a prominent pink stripe. These trailing skirts represent the vibrant tail feathers of the bird of paradise. When grasped and extended by the dancers' hands, the fabric transforms into wings; as the dancers run across the performance space, the fluttering textiles generate an illusion of aerial flight.

### Occasions and Meaning
Rooted in the natural world and Balinese cosmology, Cendrawasih draws upon the mythic status of the bird of paradise as manuk dewata—the celestial bird of the gods. Outside of local cultural displays in Bali, the dance serves as a premier showcase piece for Indonesian cultural diplomacy abroad. It has been featured at major international events, including performances in Peru in 2002, at the Freer Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C. in 2008, and across stage venues in Japan and the Netherlands.

### Notable Figures
Key historic figures associated with Cendrawasih include I Gde Manik, the visionary Buleleng choreographer who created the original 1920s variant, and N. L. N. Swasthi Wijaya Bandem, who fundamentally re-envisioned and canonized the contemporary choreography in 1988.

movement_profile.posture: Upright, delicate, with expressive head tilts and en pointe balance poses.
movement_profile.footwork: Includes standing en pointe and light fluttering running steps across the floor.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Arms extend wide holding long flowing skirts or scarves to imitate bird wings.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Flexed and responsive body posture matching avian movements.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Duet space interaction simulating avian courtship pathways.
movement_profile.partnering: Two female dancers interacting closely, representing male and female birds fluttering and flirting.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Aerobic, energetic, and rapid with sudden pauses.

signature_moves.name: Wing Extension
signature_moves.description: Holding extended skirt edges to form wide avian wing structures.

signature_moves.name: En Pointe Pose
signature_moves.description: Rising en pointe to represent perching or hovering birds.

signature_moves.name: Flight Run
signature_moves.description: Rapid running patterns that cause trailing pink-striped scarves to flutter behind.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Rises to en pointe stance; no dramatic high jumps described.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid rigid arm holds that collapse the fabric wings or heavy steps that disrupt the buoyant flight illusion.

The courtship narrative: dynamic spatial interaction between male and female bird interpretations.
